glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Solomon answers the question “what is good for man” with sayings that commend sober wisdom, patience, and trust in God’s ordering of prosperity and adversity, then shows wisdom’s limits in unjust outcomes, universal sin, and his own failed search.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Chapter 7 opens Ecclesiastes 7:1–8:17, the movement on the value and limits of wisdom. Its “better” sayings answer the question that closed chapter 6: “who knows what is good for man in life” (6:12).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “In the day of prosperity be joyful, But in the day of adversity consider: Surely God has appointed the one as well as the other, So that man can find out nothing that will come after him.” (Ecclesiastes 7:14)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Chapter 6 ended by asking what is good for a person in his short life. Ecclesiastes 7 answers with a string of comparisons that sound backward at first: “the day of death than the day of one’s birth,” and “the house of mourning” rather than “the house of feasting” (verses 1–2). The point is not that sadness is holy. A funeral makes the living “take it to heart” that life ends, while the laughter of fools is as brief and noisy as “the crackling of thorns under a pot” (verse 6). Wisdom faces reality, welcomes correction, waits patiently, and stops longing for the good old days. It also accepts that God has appointed both prosperity and adversity (verse 14).

Then Solomon turns to what wisdom cannot do. He has seen “a just man who perishes in his righteousness” and a wicked man who lives long (verse 15). If visible outcomes are all that count, the safe course is to avoid both costly righteousness and ruinous wickedness (verses 16–17). Verse 18 brings in what that calculation leaves out: “he who fears God will escape them all.” The one who fears God no longer obeys by weighing what righteousness might cost him. Reverence toward God becomes the reason for obedience, and so he escapes the trap of both extremes. The passage never permits a measured amount of sin. In fact, “there is not a just man on earth who does good And does not sin” (verse 20).

The chapter closes with Solomon’s own confession. “I said, ‘I will be wise’; But it was far from me” (verse 23). Read against 1 Kings 11, where his many wives turned his heart after other gods, the king who looked for satisfaction outside God’s will was caught in the very snare he describes (verse 26). His final discovery reaches every human being: “God made man upright, But they have sought out many schemes” (verse 29).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 7:1–6 — Better the House of Mourning Than the House of Feasting

A good name outlasts fine perfume, and the house of mourning teaches the living to take death to heart in a way the house of feasting never can. The rebuke of the wise is better than the songs of fools, whose laughter flares and dies like burning thorns.

Ecclesiastes 7:7–10 — Patience Instead of Anger and Longing for the Past

Oppression and bribes can corrupt even a wise person’s judgment, so patience is better than pride, and anger belongs to fools. Solomon also warns against asking why the former days were better than these, because that question does not come from wisdom.

Ecclesiastes 7:11–14 — Wisdom’s Protection and the Work of God

Wisdom protects as money does, but it does more, for it gives life to those who have it. No one can straighten what God has made crooked, so in prosperity a person should rejoice and in adversity remember that God has appointed both, leaving people unable to know what will come after them.

Ecclesiastes 7:15–18 — Earthly Expediency and the Fear of God

Solomon has seen a just man perish in his righteousness and a wicked man live long, and from that earthly view comes the calculating advice to be neither overly righteous nor overly wicked. Verse 18 brings the fear of God into view as what that calculation leaves out, and the book’s final answer comes in 12:13–14.

Ecclesiastes 7:19–22 — Wisdom’s Strength and the Sin of Every Person

Wisdom gives more strength than ten rulers of a city, yet no one on earth does good without sinning. Remembering how often he has cursed others, a person should not take to heart every curse he overhears.

Ecclesiastes 7:23–25 — Wisdom Beyond Reach

Solomon tested everything by wisdom and resolved to be wise, but the wisdom he sought stayed far from him, deeper than anyone can find. Still he set his heart to understand wisdom and to know the wickedness of folly.

Ecclesiastes 7:26–29 — The Snare Solomon Found and Humanity’s Many Schemes

Solomon finds more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and nets, from whom the one who pleases God escapes. Read against his own many wives and concubines (1 Kings 11:1–8), his failed search exposes his disobedience, not the inferiority of women, and his final finding applies to all people: God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 7 shows that wisdom looks at life honestly. Thinking about death, accepting correction, and waiting patiently make a person wiser than laughter and nostalgia can. In both good days and hard days, believers can trust that God has appointed both, even when they cannot see what lies ahead (7:14).

The chapter also refuses to make righteousness a safe investment. A righteous person may perish in spite of his righteousness while a wicked person lives long (7:15). When outcomes are the only measure, a person starts calculating how much obedience is worth the cost. The fear of God answers that calculation (7:18; 12:13–14), and it never permits a measured amount of sin.

Finally, Solomon admits his own failure. The wisest king could not reach the wisdom he wanted, and his own disobedience trapped him. His diagnosis in verse 29 applies to everyone, and it prepares the reader to look for a wisdom greater than Solomon’s, which the wider witness of Scripture finds in Christ (Matthew 12:42; 1 Corinthians 1:30).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Better things. A good name, honest mourning, correction, patience, and contentment with the present are better than their shallow counterparts (7:1–10).

God’s work in every season. God appoints both prosperity and adversity, and no one can straighten what He has made crooked (7:13–14).

Earthly calculation and the fear of God. Unjust outcomes tempt people to calculate how much righteousness is safe. The one who fears God escapes that whole calculation, because reverence for God, not earthly cost, becomes the reason for obedience; this is not a promise of escape from every loss (7:15–18).

Universal sin. Wisdom is strong, yet no one does good without sinning (7:19–22, 29).

Wisdom beyond reach. Solomon could not attain the full wisdom he sought, and his own search led him into a snare (7:23–28).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The house of mourning (7:2, 4). A home where people grieve a death. Going there reminds the living that death is “the end of all men,” though the passage does not command constant sadness.

What He has made crooked (7:13). Circumstances God has ordered that no human effort can straighten. The phrase recalls 1:15 and does not make God the author of moral evil.

Overly righteous (7:16). Part of the expedient advice that follows when survival is the only measure. Solomon has just seen a righteous man perish and a wicked man live long (verse 15), so verses 16–17 voice the calculation that follows: avoid righteousness that costs too much and wickedness that brings early ruin. Verse 18 then answers that calculation with the fear of God. Many interpreters take verse 16 instead as a warning against self-righteousness. Neither reading allows a measured amount of sin.

Fears God (7:18). A right view of God that shows itself in reverence, trust, and obedience. Here it is the answer to calculating how much righteousness is safe.

One man among a thousand (7:28). The thousand recalls Solomon’s seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines (1 Kings 11:3), though Ecclesiastes does not say so outright. The numbers record the failure of his own search, not a statistic about men and women.

Many schemes (7:29). The devices people invent after turning from the upright way God made them. Solomon’s final diagnosis applies to all humanity.

focus: Ecclesiastes 7 opens the movement on wisdom’s value and limits (7:1–8:17) with a run of “better” sayings that answer the closing question of 6:12, “who knows what is good for man in life.” The chapter then moves from wisdom’s real benefits to its limits: earthly calculation in the face of unjust outcomes, the universality of sin, wisdom that remains “far from me,” and Solomon’s own failed search, which ends with the diagnosis that “God made man upright, But they have sought out many schemes.”

sections.title: Better the House of Mourning Than the House of Feasting
sections.summary: A good name and the day of death are better than precious ointment and the day of birth, because the house of mourning teaches the living to “take it to heart.” The rebuke of the wise is better than “the song of fools,” whose laughter is like “the crackling of thorns under a pot.”

sections.title: Patience Instead of Anger and Longing for the Past
sections.summary: Oppression and bribes can corrupt even a wise man’s judgment, so “The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.” Solomon warns against quick anger and against asking, “Why were the former days better than these?”

sections.title: Wisdom’s Protection and the Work of God
sections.summary: Wisdom is good with an inheritance and “gives life to those who have it,” yet no one can “make straight what He has made crooked.” In prosperity a person should be joyful, and in adversity he should consider that God has appointed both, “So that man can find out nothing that will come after him.”

sections.summary: Solomon has seen “a just man who perishes in his righteousness” and a wicked man who lives long, and from that earthly horizon comes the calculated counsel not to be “overly righteous” or “overly wicked.” Verse 18 brings the fear of God into view: “he who fears God will escape them all.”

sections.title: The Snare Solomon Found and Humanity’s Many Schemes
sections.summary: Solomon finds “more bitter than death” the woman whose heart is snares and nets, from whom “He who pleases God shall escape.” Searching one thing after another, he found one man among a thousand but no woman, and he concludes that “God made man upright, But they have sought out many schemes.”

1.brief: Solomon begins a series of “better” sayings by valuing “a good name,” the lasting reputation of a person’s character, above “precious ointment,” the fragrant luxury of a feast. He adds that the day of death is better than the day of birth, because at death a life’s course is complete and its true worth can be seen, while a birth only begins that course.
1.explain:
A good name is better than precious ointment, begins a series of “better” comparisons that answer the question Solomon left open in 6:12, “who knows what is good for man in life.” A name stands for a person’s reputation and character as others know them. Precious ointment was perfumed oil used at feasts and on special occasions, a sign of luxury and celebration. Solomon values the lasting fragrance of a good character above the passing fragrance of expensive perfume.

And the day of death than the day of one’s birth; is a surprising comparison. A birth opens a life with all its possibilities still unknown, while death closes it, so that its true character and worth can finally be seen. The verse does not despise life or praise death for its own sake. It reflects on the fact that a life is weighed by how it ends, the same point Solomon makes in verse 8: “The end of a thing is better than its beginning.”
1.notes: In Hebrew, “name” (shem) and “ointment” (shemen) sound almost alike, so the first line contains a play on words that links a good name with fine perfume.

2.brief: It is better to visit the house where people mourn than the house of feasting, because death “is the end of all men,” and the living who face it “will take it to heart.” Mourning teaches what celebration lets people forget: life is short and must be lived wisely.
2.explain:
Better to go to the house of mourning Than to go to the house of feasting, contrasts two places a person might visit. The house of mourning is a home where someone has died and family and friends gather to grieve. The house of feasting is a place of celebration and plenty. Solomon says the first is the better visit.

For that is the end of all men; gives the reason. Death is the destination of every human life, and the house of mourning makes that fact impossible to ignore.

And the living will take it to heart. shows what mourning teaches. Those who stand beside a grave are moved to reflect on their own lives and to live with wisdom while they can. A feast can help people forget their mortality; a funeral reminds them of it.

3.brief: “Sorrow is better than laughter” because grief honestly faced can make the heart better, deepening understanding in a way that easy amusement cannot. The verse does not command constant sadness; it values the sober reflection that sorrow brings.
3.explain:
Sorrow is better than laughter, continues the comparisons. “Sorrow” here is grief or sadness, the kind that comes when people face loss honestly. “Laughter” is the light amusement that passes quickly.

For by a sad countenance the heart is made better. explains why. A sad face reflects a heart that is taking life seriously, and grief honestly faced can deepen understanding and soften the heart. The verse does not command constant sadness or condemn joy, which Solomon commends elsewhere as God’s gift (8:15; 9:7). It values the sober reflection that sorrow can produce.
3.notes: The NLT renders the second line, “for sadness has a refining influence on us,” which brings out the idea that sorrow can improve character.

4.brief: The wise keep their hearts where life is weighed seriously, in “the house of mourning,” while fools set their hearts on “the house of mirth,” seeking only diversion. The contrast is about what each kind of person attends to and learns from.
4.explain:
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, describes where the wise keep their attention. Even when they are not literally at a funeral, their hearts dwell on the lessons of mortality and of life’s brevity.

But the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. sets the fool beside him. The fool’s heart is fixed on amusement and diversion. The difference between the two lies in what each attends to and learns from.

5.brief: Hearing the honest rebuke of a wise person is better than listening to “the song of fools,” however pleasant it sounds. Correction may hurt, but it does good that flattery and empty entertainment never do.
5.explain:
It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise turns from mourning to correction. A rebuke is an honest word that exposes a fault. Coming from a wise person, it may sting, but it can lead to real change.

Than for a man to hear the song of fools. names the alternative. The song of fools may be pleasant entertainment or flattery, but it does nothing to make a person better. Solomon values hard truth spoken by the wise above easy pleasure offered by fools.

6.brief: The laughter of fools is like “the crackling of thorns under a pot,” loud and quick but producing little heat and soon gone. Solomon calls this “vanity,” empty and fleeting.
6.explain:
For like the crackling of thorns under a pot, gives a picture from everyday life. Dry thorns burned under a cooking pot catch quickly, crackle loudly, and burn out fast, giving little lasting heat.

So is the laughter of the fool. applies the picture. The fool’s laughter is noisy but short-lived and accomplishes little.

This also is vanity. closes the opening group of sayings. The word “vanity” describes something fleeting and empty, like a breath. Here it may apply to the fool’s laughter, or to the whole contrast between wisdom and folly drawn in verses 1–6.
6.notes: The Hebrew words for “thorns” (sirim) and “pot” (sir) sound alike, so the comparison itself makes a play on sound, as noisy as the crackling it describes.

7.brief: Even a wise man can be corrupted: oppression can drive him to irrational responses, and “a bribe debases the heart,” bending his judgment. Wisdom does not make anyone immune to pressure or gain, which is why patience and integrity matter.
7.explain:
Surely oppression destroys a wise man’s reason, warns that wisdom does not make a person immune to pressure. Oppression, whether suffering it or wielding it, can unsettle judgment and drive even a wise person to act foolishly.

And a bribe debases the heart. adds a second danger. A bribe corrupts the inner person, bending judgment toward personal gain. This verse explains why the patience and integrity commended in the following verses matter so much.
7.notes: Some interpreters connect verse 7 with the sayings before it, as an example of how wisdom can be lost; others read it with verses 8–10. The verse stands between the two groups and links them.

8.brief: The outcome of a matter shows its worth better than its beginning, so “The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.” Patience waits to see how things end, while pride rushes ahead and refuses to wait.
8.explain:
The end of a thing is better than its beginning; takes up the theme of verse 1. The outcome of a matter shows its real value, while beginnings can be misleading.

The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. draws the lesson. A patient person waits to see how things turn out and does not react rashly, while pride rushes ahead, insists on its own way, and refuses to wait.

9.brief: Solomon warns against being quick to anger, “For anger rests in the bosom of fools.” A fool holds anger close and lets it settle in, while the wise keep it from taking hold.
9.explain:
Do not hasten in your spirit to be angry, warns against a quick temper. Being slow to anger is a mark of the patient spirit just commended.

For anger rests in the bosom of fools. gives the reason. The fool does not merely feel anger; he holds it close and lets it settle in his heart. The wise refuse to let anger take up residence.

10.brief: Do not ask why former days were better than these, because that complaint is not a wise question. Longing for an idealized past can keep a person from facing the present faithfully.
10.explain:
Do not say, “Why were the former days better than these?” addresses a common complaint. People often idealize the past and use it to criticize the present.

For you do not inquire wisely concerning this. explains why the question is unwise. It assumes the past was better, which may not be true, and it keeps a person from facing present responsibilities faithfully. Wisdom deals with life as it is now.

11.brief: “Wisdom is good with an inheritance,” and it profits “those who see the sun,” that is, the living. Wisdom joined with an inheritance is a real advantage in this life, because wisdom knows how to use well what has been received.
11.explain:
Wisdom is good with an inheritance, affirms that wisdom joined with an inheritance makes a strong combination. An inheritance provides resources, and wisdom knows how to use well what has been received.

And profitable to those who see the sun. shows who benefits. “Those who see the sun” are the living. Wisdom gives a real advantage in this life.
11.notes: The Hebrew can also be read as comparing wisdom with an inheritance rather than joining the two. The NIV takes it that way: “Wisdom, like an inheritance, is a good thing.” The NLT, displayed above, follows the sense of combination, and this study follows the NKJV reading of wisdom joined with an inheritance.

12.brief: Wisdom gives protection as money does, but it has a greater excellence: “wisdom gives life to those who have it.” Money can shelter a person for a time, while wisdom guides and preserves life itself.
12.explain:
For wisdom is a defense as money is a defense, explains the value of verse 11. Both wisdom and money offer protection, like shade from the heat. Money can shelter a person from many troubles, and so can good judgment.

But the excellence of knowledge is that wisdom gives life to those who have it. names the greater advantage. Money can protect only so far, but wisdom preserves and guides life itself. Its benefit reaches the whole person.
12.notes: The Hebrew behind “defense” literally speaks of shade, a common image for protection in a hot land.

13.brief: Solomon calls the reader to “Consider the work of God,” for no one can straighten what God has made crooked. People must accept that God’s ordering of circumstances lies beyond their power to rearrange.
13.explain:
Consider the work of God; calls the reader to look carefully at what God does. The search now turns explicitly to God’s ordering of events.

For who can make straight what He has made crooked? repeats a thought from 1:15. Some circumstances in life are bent in ways no human effort can straighten. Solomon attributes this to God’s work, meaning that He orders the course of events. The verse does not make God the author of moral evil; it calls people to accept what lies beyond their control.

14.brief: In good days a person should be joyful, and in hard days he should stop and consider that God has appointed both. God mixes prosperity and adversity so that no one can know what will come next, which keeps people humble and dependent on Him.
14.explain:
In the day of prosperity be joyful, tells the reader how to respond when life goes well: receive it with gladness.

But in the day of adversity consider: calls for reflection when life is hard. Adversity is a time to stop and think.

Surely God has appointed the one as well as the other, states what reflection discovers. Both prosperity and adversity come within God’s appointment.

So that man can find out nothing that will come after him. gives God’s purpose. By mixing good days and hard days, God keeps people from predicting or controlling their future. This keeps them humble and dependent on Him.

15.brief: Solomon reports what he has seen in his “days of vanity”: a righteous man who dies despite his righteousness and a wicked man who lives long in his wickedness. This observation frustrates the simple expectation that righteousness always brings survival and wickedness an early end.
15.explain:
I have seen everything in my days of vanity: introduces a hard observation. “Days of vanity” refers to Solomon’s fleeting life, the brief span in which he made his search.

There is a just man who perishes in his righteousness, reports the first case. A righteous person dies, and his righteousness did not save him from an early death.

And there is a wicked man who prolongs life in his wickedness. reports the second case. A wicked person lives a long life despite his evil. These observations frustrate the simple expectation that righteousness always brings a long life and wickedness an early death.

16.brief: From that earthly horizon comes a calculated counsel: do not be “overly righteous” or “overly wise,” lest you destroy yourself. Solomon is voicing where expediency leads when visible outcomes are the only measure: avoid righteousness that costs too much.
16.explain:
Do not be overly righteous, is the first part of a counsel that follows from verse 15. Solomon is best understood here as voicing the calculation that arises when visible outcomes are the only measure. If righteousness can lead to an early death, the expedient course is to avoid righteousness that costs too much.

Nor be overly wise: extends the same reasoning to wisdom. Too much commitment to wisdom might also bring trouble.

Why should you destroy yourself? states the motive of this counsel: self-preservation. Solomon is exposing where earthly calculation leads. It produces a morality measured only by personal safety. The passage does not teach that believers should hold back from obedience.
16.notes: Some interpreters read verse 16 differently, as a warning against self-righteousness, legalism, or pride in one’s own wisdom. The Hebrew form translated “overly wise” can carry the sense of making oneself out to be wise. On either reading the passage does not commend moderation in obedience.

17.brief: The same calculation warns against being “overly wicked” or foolish, lest a person die before his time. Within this reasoning, wickedness is avoided not because it offends God but because it brings early ruin, which exposes how thin such morality is.
17.explain:
Do not be overly wicked, completes the calculation of someone whose only aim is self-preservation. In that reasoning, wickedness is avoided only when it goes too far. This is not permission for a little wickedness; it shows how shallow morality becomes when personal safety is the only measure.

Nor be foolish: adds folly to the warning.

Why should you die before your time? again gives self-preservation as the motive. In this reasoning, excessive wickedness is avoided because it brings early ruin, not because it offends God. The counsel exposes how thin such morality is when outcomes are the only measure.

18.brief: Solomon says it is good to hold on to this and not let go of the other, and then brings the fear of God into view: “he who fears God will escape them all.” The one who reverences God is not guided by calculation but by a right relationship with Him, and that is the book’s answer.
18.explain:
It is good that you grasp this, refers to the counsel of the preceding verses.

And also not remove your hand from the other; urges holding on to both warnings together.

For he who fears God will escape them all. brings the fear of God into view. The person who reverences God is guided not by calculation but by a right relationship with Him, and he escapes the extremes that calculation tries to manage. Here the book’s answer begins to appear, an answer stated fully in 12:13–14: “Fear God and keep His commandments.”
18.notes: The Hebrew of verse 18 is compact, and translations differ on whether “this” and “the other” refer to the two warnings of verses 16–17 or to the righteous and wicked of verse 15.

19.brief: Wisdom strengthens the wise more than ten rulers of a city could, giving more protection than a whole council of powerful men. Its value lies in the strength of good judgment, not in numbers or position.
19.explain:
Wisdom strengthens the wise turns to a new saying about wisdom’s value.

More than ten rulers of the city. gives a comparison. Ten rulers picture substantial civic power, many men of authority within one city. The number makes a comparison rather than describing how many officials a city had. Wisdom gives the wise person more strength and protection than such powerful men could provide.

20.brief: Yet wisdom has its limit, because “there is not a just man on earth who does good And does not sin.” Every person, however wise or righteous, falls short and needs God’s mercy.
20.explain:
For there is not a just man on earth who does good qualifies the praise of wisdom with a sober truth.

And does not sin. completes the statement. No one, however wise or righteous, lives without sin. This universal truth humbles every person and reminds the wise that wisdom does not make them sinless.
20.notes: Solomon prayed in similar words at the dedication of the temple: “for there is no one who does not sin” (1 Kings 8:46).

21.brief: Do not take to heart everything people say, or you may overhear even your own servant cursing you. A wise person does not live by every remark made about him.
21.explain:
Also do not take to heart everything people say, gives practical counsel. A wise person does not hang on every remark made about him.

Lest you hear your servant cursing you. gives an example. If a person listens to everything, he may overhear even his own servant speaking against him. Some things are better not pursued.

22.brief: Your own heart knows that you have often cursed others as well. Remembering his own careless words helps a person respond to others’ words with restraint and humility.
22.explain:
For many times, also, your own heart has known calls for honest self-examination.

That even you have cursed others. gives the reason for restraint. Everyone has spoken carelessly about others. Remembering one’s own faults leads to humility and patience when others speak unkindly.

23.brief: Solomon tested all of this by wisdom and resolved, “I will be wise,” yet the wisdom he sought “was far from me.” The wisest of kings confesses that complete understanding remained beyond his reach.
23.explain:
All this I have proved by wisdom. summarizes Solomon’s method. He tested these matters through careful reflection.

I said, “I will be wise”; records his resolution. He set out to gain complete wisdom.

But it was far from me. records his failure. Even Solomon, the wisest of kings, found that the complete understanding he sought remained beyond his reach.

24.brief: What lies “far off and exceedingly deep” cannot be fully found out by anyone. Solomon recognizes that the deepest reasons of things are beyond human searching.
24.explain:
As for that which is far off and exceedingly deep, describes the object of his search: the deepest reasons of things, distant and profound.

Who can find it out? is a question that expects the answer “no one.” The full understanding of life and God’s work lies beyond human discovery.

25.brief: Still, Solomon applied his heart to search out wisdom and “the reason of things,” and to understand the wickedness of folly and madness. His search continued, and it now turns to what he found in his own life.
25.explain:
I applied my heart to know, resumes the account of Solomon’s search.

To search and seek out wisdom and the reason of things, describes its aim. He wanted to understand the explanation behind events.

To know the wickedness of folly, Even of foolishness and madness. adds another aim. He sought to understand folly and its destructive nature. This verse introduces what he found in the following verses.

26.brief: Solomon finds “more bitter than death” the woman whose heart is snares and nets and whose hands are fetters, and he says that one who pleases God will escape her while the sinner is caught. Read against Solomon’s own compromised relationships (1 Kings 11:1–8), the verse records the snare he himself fell into.
26.explain:
And I find more bitter than death introduces a painful discovery, something worse than death itself.

The woman whose heart is snares and nets, Whose hands are fetters. describes a woman who entraps, using images of hunting and captivity. The passage is best read against Solomon’s own life: his many foreign wives turned his heart away from God (1 Kings 11:1–8). The king who sought satisfaction outside God’s will became caught in the snare he describes.

He who pleases God shall escape from her, shows the way of escape. The one who pleases God is kept from this trap.

But the sinner shall be trapped by her. states the opposite outcome. Solomon’s own history shows the truth of this warning.
26.notes: First Kings 11:3 records that Solomon “had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines; and his wives turned away his heart.” Verse 4 adds the separate account of his later years: when he was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods.

27.brief: Speaking of the Preacher in the third person, the book reports his method: he added one thing to another to find the reason. Solomon’s search was careful and deliberate, not careless.
27.explain:
Here is what I have found, introduces Solomon’s report of what his careful search turned up.

says the Preacher, is one of the book’s third-person references to the Preacher (1:1–2; 7:27; 12:8–10). These words frame Solomon’s report without signaling another author.

Adding one thing to the other to find out the reason, describes his method. He put observations together one by one, seeking the explanation of things.
27.notes: This is the only place in the body of the book where the Preacher is referred to in the third person; the other references come in the opening and closing frame (1:1–2; 12:8–10).

28.brief: What his soul still sought he could not find: he found one man among a thousand, but not a woman among them. Read against the seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines of 1 Kings 11:3, the verse reflects the failure of Solomon’s own search, not a verdict on women in general.
28.explain:
Which my soul still seeks but I cannot find: admits that his search remains incomplete.

One man among a thousand I have found, reports a rare discovery of one man among a thousand.

But a woman among all these I have not found. reports that he found no woman. The thousand most likely recalls Solomon’s own seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines (1 Kings 11:3), though Ecclesiastes does not say so outright. The verse exposes the failure of his own disobedient search; it is not a verdict on women in general or a statistic about men and women.

29.brief: Solomon’s one sure finding is that “God made man upright, But they have sought out many schemes.” The problem lies not with God’s design but with all humanity, men and women alike, who have turned to their own devices.
29.explain:
Truly, this only I have found: introduces Solomon’s one sure conclusion.

That God made man upright, affirms that God created humanity good and morally straight.

But they have sought out many schemes. names the cause of human corruption. People have turned from God’s design to their own devices. This conclusion widens the diagnosis from Solomon’s own failure to all humanity, men and women alike.
29.notes: The Hebrew word translated “man” in verse 29 is the general term for humanity (adam), and the following “they” confirms that all people are in view.
